headline: Mishin is simply from English “sewing machine”.
Hakike is haki, the stem of 吐く (haku, “vomit”), plus 気 (-ke, “feeling”).
Sunao is, by surface analysis, 素 (su, “plain”) plus 直 (nao, “straight”).
Sakasa is a clipping of 逆様 (sakasama), of the same meaning.
Mittomonai is a vowel shortening and gemination of みとうもない (mitōmonai), from みたくもない (mitakumonai, “don't even want to see”).
Maniau is 間 (ma, “spatial interval, temporal interval”) plus に (ni) plus 合う (au, “to match, to fit”).
Yakeru is from Old Japanese 焼く (yaku), in the lower bigrade pattern.
Konshū, “this week”, began as konsiu.
Ranbō is ran (乱, disordered, confused, chaotic) plus bō (暴, acting with destructive force).
Toshin is 都 (to, “metropolis”) plus 心 (shin, “central part”).
Oku is rooted in Old Japanese despite overlapping with a goon reading from Middle Chinese, and is cognate with 沖 (oki, “the open sea, offshore”).
Makura is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE, and has Proto-Ryukyuan cognates such as Okinawan makkwa.
Dekiagaru is deki, the stem of 出来る (dekiru), plus 上がる (agaru, “to go up, come to an end”).
Kuyashii is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, ultimately from the classical verb 悔ゆ (kuyu, “to regret”).
Ta, “rice field”, appears in the Kojiki of roughly 711-712, from Proto-Japonic *ta.
Bōya is 坊 (bō, “boy”) plus や (ya, interjectory particle); its resemblance to English boy is coincidental.
Bōsan is from お坊さん (obōsan).
Pasu has three borrowings behind it: English pass, a clipping of カリパス (karipasu) from calipers, and English path.
Gimon is Middle Chinese 疑問, literally “doubt, suspicion + ask”, first attested in the early 1600s.
Ude is from Proto-Japonic *untai, cognate with Okinawan 腕 (udi).
Fue went from puye through ɸue to fue, and is likely related to the verb 吹く (fuku, “to blow”).
Chikarazuyoi is 力 (chikara, “power, strength”) plus 強い (tsuyoi), with tsuyoi voiced to zuyoi.
Yoake is 夜 (yo, “night”) plus 明け (ake, “end (of a period)”).
Hōru took five steps from papur to hōru.
Osu, “to push”, is a doublet of 推す (osu).
Sō is a clipping of 僧伽 (sōgya), borrowed from Sanskrit saṃgha.
Kawa, “leather”, is a specialization of 皮 (kawa, “skin”).
Tsukiai is the stem of 付き合う (tsukiau, “keep company with”), equivalent to 付き (tsuki) plus 合い (ai).
Katazuke is the continuative stem of 片付ける (katazukeru, “to tidy up”).
Jūyō is Middle Chinese 重要, literally “heavy + important”.
